Project: Space Observation Project 1, Group 2 (study deck)
Lecturer: Dr. Nguyen Thi Phuong
USTH, Master 2 Space, November 2026
1  Introduction. What is in this deck?
The template
Huang et al. 2018 (TESS discovery of π Men c) shows five figure types. We redraw them for our ten planets from public TESS data.
The plots
33 new figures. Each slide says what the image shows, with measured numbers.
The authors
Our ten planets against their discovery papers: same numbers or not, and why.
The literature
150 verified papers in eleven sub-methods; 144 open-access PDFs downloaded.

Everything is computed from public data: TESS SPOC light curves (MAST) and the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Section 3 tells how exoplanets have been found, section 4 gives the TESS numbers with their sources, section 5 asks whether ten planets are enough, and section 10 shows how to retrieve each number.

3  Methods. One image series, three uses: differential photometry, centroiding, and calibration for imaging
Differential photometry
The flux of the star falls by (R<sub>p</sub>/R<sub>★</sub>)<sup>2</sup> when a planet crosses it. TESS: yes; this is all ten of our planets, 23 to 170 points per transit.

The (x, y) position of the star moves when a blended star dips, or when a planet pulls the star. TESS uses it as a test (Ricker Sec 8.2: transit-specific image motion). We measured shifts of at most 0.027″.
Calibration for imaging
A coronagraph hides the star; short unsaturated frames of the star still locate its centre so that its diffraction halo can be subtracted. TESS has no coronagraph.
The same frames serve very different methods; what changes is what is measured on them.
Source: Ricker 2015 Sec 8.2; our centroid test (code/33_checkpoint_facts.py)

3  Methods. Transit photometry and the four numbers: many stars, a coarse pixel, 2-min points, a sector of 27 days
1  Field of view

Needs: hundreds of thousands of stars: the geometric probability is only about 5 % (Ricker p. 4), at least 500 stars per super-Earth (Ricker p. 4)
TESS: 24° × 96° = 2300 deg², at least 200 000 targets
2  Spatial resolution

Needs: no need to separate planet and star, only to collect the star's light
TESS: 21″ pixels; our apertures 13 to 31 pixels; CROWDSAP down to 0.42
3  Temporal resolution

Needs: a point every few minutes through a dip of hours
TESS: 0.8 to 5.7 h transits: 23 to 170 points at 2 min
4  Revisit time

Needs: two transits at least, to give a period
TESS: 27.4 d sector: 4.5 to 98 transits for P = 6.1 to 0.28 d
The survey numbers (wide field, coarse pixel) are exactly what a low transit probability asks for.
Source: Ricker 2015 Sec 3.5, Table 1; our fits (results/checkpoint_geometry.csv)
3  Methods. Phase curve and secondary eclipse and the four numbers: bright hot hosts, one pixel, 2 min, many orbits

Needs: a rare planet: very hot, giant, close, around a bright star
TESS: 2300 deg² gives WASP-18 (T mag 8.8) and a few like it

Needs: star and planet in the same aperture, the total flux of the system
TESS: separation 0.16 mas against a 21″ pixel: always blended, as wanted

Needs: enough points to bin down to tens of ppm over a 0.94-d orbit
TESS: 2 min gives 678 points per orbit; we measured 352 ± 9 ppm at phase 0.5

Needs: many consecutive orbits without a day-night gap
TESS: 29 orbits in 27.4 d, uninterrupted except for the downlink gap
The phase curve uses the coarse pixel as an advantage: nothing is lost outside the aperture.
Source: Ricker 2015 Table 1; Shporer 2019; our fits and phase-0.5 measurement
3  Methods. False-positive vetting and the four numbers: neighbours, sub-pixel centroids, equal sampling, enough transits

Needs: neighbouring stars in the same field to compare against
TESS: the stamp holds the target and its neighbours; CROWDSAP tells how many

Needs: sub-pixel position of the light centre
TESS: centroid error 0.0010 to 0.010″ per planet, measured

Needs: the same sampling for odd and even transits
TESS: one 2-min cadence for all; odd-even test done on the ten

Needs: several transits of each parity
TESS: 4 to 84 transits per planet
Vetting uses the pixel grid as information: where the light sits, not what the planet looks like.
Source: SPOC centroids (MOM_CENTR1, 2) of our files; our fits (results/checkpoint_vetting.csv)
3  Methods. Asteroseismology and the four numbers: many bright stars, disc-integrated light, 2 min or 20 s, long stares

Needs: many bright stars of every age
TESS: p-modes expected on about 6 000 stars (Ricker p. 12)

Needs: only the total light of the star
TESS: disc-integrated brightness: the 21″ pixel does no harm

Needs: a Nyquist frequency above νmax of the star
TESS: 2 min: 4 167 µHz; 20 s: 25 000; 30 min: 278 (too low for Sun-like stars)

Needs: long uninterrupted data: frequency resolution = 1/T
TESS: 27.4 d: 0.42 µHz; over 300 d near the poles: below 0.039 µHz (Ricker p. 11)
The fast cadence is the decisive number here; full frames at 30 min cannot see Sun-like p-modes.
Source: Ricker 2015 Sec 7.2, 8.3; Huber 2011 Sec 2; Nyquist and resolution computed
3  Methods. Stars in full frames and the four numbers: a million objects per image, coarse pixels in sparse fields, 30 min to 200 s

Needs: the whole field, no pre-selection
TESS: Ricker p. 13: any bright star in 2300 deg²

Needs: separate stars from their neighbours
TESS: 21″ works where stars are sparse; limited where crowded (our reasoning)

Needs: events of minutes to weeks: flares, eclipses, novae (our reasoning)
TESS: 30 min, then 10 min, then 200 s

Needs: a continuous record through each event
TESS: 27.4 d per sector, 2 years for the whole sky
Full frames trade a longer cadence for coverage of every star, which is what variable-star work wants.
Source: Ricker 2015 Table 1, Sec 8.4; NASA HEASARC data products page

3  Methods. Transit photometry, step by step: fold, search, fit, then radius, geometry and stellar density
φ = ( (t − T<sub>0</sub>) mod P ) / P ;  BLS strength = √[ n<sub>in</sub>n<sub>out</sub> / (n<sub>in</sub> + n<sub>out</sub>) ] ( ⟨f⟩<sub>out</sub> − ⟨f⟩<sub>in</sub> ) / σ
1. Fold on a trial period; the best (P, T<sub>0</sub>, duration) is the BLS peak. Input: the 1-D series f(t).

z(t) = (a/R<sub>★</sub>) √[ sin<sup>2</sup>θ + cos<sup>2</sup>i cos<sup>2</sup>θ ] ,  θ = 2π(t − T<sub>0</sub>)/P ;  I(μ) = I<sub>0</sub> [ 1 − u<sub>1</sub>(1 − μ) − u<sub>2</sub>(1 − μ)<sup>2</sup> ]
2. Mandel-Agol model with quadratic limb darkening, fitted by MCMC (our pipeline).
δ ≈ (R<sub>p</sub>/R<sub>★</sub>)<sup>2</sup> ,  R<sub>p</sub> = R<sub>★</sub> √δ ;  b = (a/R<sub>★</sub>) cos i
3. Radius. Example HD 118203 b: R<sub>p</sub>/R<sub>★</sub> = 0.0553, R<sub>★</sub> = 2.04 R<sub>☉</sub> gives 12.30 R<sub>⊕</sub>.
a/R<sub>★</sub> = √[ (1 + k)<sup>2</sup> − b<sup>2</sup> cos<sup>2</sup>(πT<sub>14</sub>/P) ] / sin(πT<sub>14</sub>/P) ;  ρ<sub>★</sub> = 3π (a/R<sub>★</sub>)<sup>3</sup> / (G P<sup>2</sup>)
4. Geometry and density. The form without the cos<sup>2</sup> term is off by up to 2.8 % (LTT 9779 b); the exact form returns b and a/R<sub>★</sub> from our fits to 10<sup>−13</sup>.

Input: the 1-D series. Z > 3 suggests an eclipsing binary at twice the period. Our result: slide on odd against even.
F<sub>ellip</sub> = −A<sub>ellip</sub> cos 4πφ ,  A<sub>ellip</sub> ∝ (M<sub>p</sub>/M<sub>★</sub>)(R<sub>★</sub>/a)<sup>3</sup> sin<sup>2</sup>i ;  F<sub>beam</sub> = A<sub>beam</sub> sin 2πφ
Input: the series folded on P. Shporer 2019 measured both for WASP-18 b; we did not.
X<sub>c</sub> = Σ x [I − B] / Σ [I − B] ,  Y<sub>c</sub> likewise ;  ΔR<sub>c</sub> = √[ (X<sub>in</sub> − X<sub>out</sub>)<sup>2</sup> + (Y<sub>in</sub> − Y<sub>out</sub>)<sup>2</sup> ]
Input: the images (flux-weighted centroids of the stamp; SPOC stores them as MOM_CENTR1 and 2). A shift > 3σ points to a blended star.

11  Questions. Likely questions and short answers
Is float32 versus float64 the cause?
No. Rounding 10<sup>-7</sup> against noise 10<sup>-4</sup>; a float32 refit moved the ratio 0.2 %, MCMC noise.
Why does Rp match for the paper's planet but not its ratio?
π Men c: our R<sub>★</sub> is 1.17, the paper's 1.10; the offsets cancel.
Why guided mode for three planets?
Blind BLS locks on aliases for low S/N or short P; the window is a restriction, the period is still fitted.
Why only the first sectors?
Run time and a clean baseline; more sectors would sharpen P, not R<sub>p</sub>.
What is β?
Ratio of measured to white-noise rms in transit-length bins; 1 means white noise.
Why not use the catalog duration?
Blind mode does not; guided mode uses it only for the BLS duration grid.
11  Questions. Ten questions the lecturer may ask: 1 to 5
Short answer and where it is shown
Why can a dip in brightness give a radius?
Depth ≈ (R<sub>p</sub>/R<sub>★</sub>)², R<sub>p</sub> = ratio × R<sub>★</sub>. R<sub>★</sub> comes from the archive, not from us, so its error goes straight into R<sub>p</sub> (section 7).
Why trust this period, not P/2 or 2P?
BLS scans 0.26 to 15 d; 8 of 10 periods agree with the catalog within 2σ. Three planets were searched near the catalog period; K2-141 b searched blind gave 5.68 d (sections 6, 7).
Where do the errors come from; are they complete?
MCMC, three detrending variants and R<sub>★</sub>. Red noise (β 1.0 to 3.6) is not included; with ×β the HD 189733 b pull falls from -2.0σ to -0.6σ (section 7).
Why does the result differ from NASA?
A difference means something only in units of its error. 9 of 10 ratios are within 2σ. Catalog values come from other papers: only 1 planet takes them from its discovery paper (section 7).
How do you know it is a planet, not a binary star?
All ten are confirmed planets in the NASA archive; we did no centroid vetting. We ran the odd-even test and the phase-0.5 test (WASP-18 b: 352 ± 9 ppm; Shporer et al. 341) (section 7).
Inferred from the group's comments (the nature of the result, why, and what supports it); the lecturer has not confirmed them.
11  Questions. Ten questions the lecturer may ask: 6 to 10
Do the ratio, the impact parameter and limb darkening degenerate?
Limb darkening (q<sub>1</sub>, q<sub>2</sub>) and b are fitted. LTT 9779 b: b = 0.91 and a 13 % error, mostly from detrending, not from MCMC (section 6).
Which assumptions can be wrong?
Circular orbits for all ten (HD 118203 b has e = 0.316, Pepper 2020), R<sub>★</sub> from the archive, only 1 to 4 sectors, and the crowding correction (LTT 1445 A b: CROWDSAP 0.42) (sections 4, 6).
What does TESS give, and what does it not?
2-min points, 27-d sectors, 21″ pixels, gaps of 1 to 8 d. Period error from 0.6 ppm (WASP-18 b) to 173 ppm (K2-141 b) (section 4).
Why these ten planets? Is ten enough?
They cover every size class and host-star type; the 7 to 15 d period class is empty (29 % of the catalog sample). Enough to show the method, not to say anything about a class (section 5).
What would you do differently?
Use every sector, fit the eccentricity, detrend with Gaussian processes, multiply the errors by β, and read the Methods of each catalog paper (sections 7, 8).

Study deck for the ten planets: figure types taken from one TESS discovery paper, plots for every planet, a comparison with the authors of each discovery paper, a verified literature review by sub-method, and how to retrieve every number.

This is a study deck, separate from the 25-minute presentation. It answers: what does the paper actually say, can we rebuild it, where do we agree with the authors, and what is the literature behind each step.

Measured is self-computed. Catalog and Published are taken from data. The stellar radius enters the radius, so compare the ratio when you want the pure light-curve result. LTT 9779 b, LTT 1445 A b and K2-141 b were searched in a window around the catalog period.

Float precision is not a cause: the SPOC file stores flux as float32 with relative rounding 1e-7, the noise is 1e-4. Sampler noise is real but small. The big ones are the stellar radius and old discovery papers.
We rebuild with our own pipeline on the same sector, so the comparison is a test of the method, not a copy of their plots.

Period and radius agree. But the depth is not the same: the paper's Figure 4 histogram peaks near 290 ppm, ours is 252 ppm, a -6.6 percent difference in the ratio. The radius matches only because the archive stellar radius 1.17 is larger than the paper's 1.10. The cause of the depth difference is not identified: candidates are detrending, SPOC data reprocessing and crowding; none tested.

Layout and drawing style follow the Hadoop timeline of the HUST sample deck (slide 31): lanes by role, dashed lines for ideas, solid lines for dependencies. Every node has a paper in the literature folder and a verbatim quote checked in data/literature/tess_fact_sources.csv. Mayor and Queloz 1995 and Wolszczan 1992 are paywalled and were not downloaded; their entries rest on the title and the Crossref record. The transit probability is about R star over a. In our ten planets it runs from 3.5 to 47 per cent, which is why a survey needs many stars; Ricker quotes 5 per cent and 500 stars per detection. The pixel only has to gather the light of one star; the 21 arcsec pixel costs us the crowding correction. Durations of 0.8 to 5.7 hours are sampled by 23 to 170 points at 2 minutes. A period below 13.7 days gives at least two transits in a sector.

WASP-18 b has P = 0.941 d, so one sector holds 29 orbits; we used four sectors and 84 transits. The planet lies 0.16 mas from its star, so planet and star always fall in the same pixel, which is what a total-flux measurement wants.

The pixel is 21 arcsec, yet the centroid test works because a centroid is an average over many electrons: our errors are 0.00005 to 0.00024 pixel in x, a few thousandths of an arcsecond. The odd-even test needs at least a few transits of each parity; our counts run from 4 to 84.

The Sun oscillates at ν<sub>max</sub> = 3090 µHz, a period of 5.4 min (Huber 2011, p. 2). The Nyquist frequency of a 2-min cadence is 1/(2 × 120 s) = 4 167 µHz, so it is seen; a 30-min cadence reaches only 278 µHz.

Each 30-min image gives about 10<sup>6</sup> bright objects and about 20 million are covered in two years (Ricker p. 14). The pixel is coarse, so the crowded Galactic plane is the weak point: 90 % of a star's light falls inside 1.4 arcmin (Ricker p. 7). Cadence by cycle is 30 min, 10 min, 200 s (NASA HEASARC).

Every method of the next slides starts here. The image cube is summed over the aperture to give SAP flux; cotrending removes shared systematics; the crowding term removes the light of neighbours; dividing by the flux fraction restores the light that fell outside the aperture. Our data say otherwise: for LTT 1445 A b the median ratio PDCSAP over SAP is 0.434, equal to C over f, whereas the other form would give 1.03.

Worked example for the phase curve. The depth at phase 0.5 is the sum of reflected and thermal light. If it were all reflected the albedo would have to be 0.42; the TESS paper limits it to below 0.048, so the secondary eclipse is mostly thermal. Solving the Planck integral over a flat 600 to 1000 nm band gives a day-side brightness temperature near 3000 K for both the published and our depth; the band is flat, so this is an approximation of ours.

Three tests, three kinds of input. Odd-even uses only the brightness series. Ellipsoidal modulation and Doppler beaming are harmonics of the orbital period and need the folded series. Full-frame work needs methods that do not rely on a fixed aperture. Difference imaging subtracts a reference image so that every constant star vanishes and only changing sources remain. The odd-even test compares depths of alternate transits; an eclipsing binary at twice the period would differ by tens of percent. Differences of 1 percent on the hot Jupiters are far too small for that. The formal significance is inflated because the errors treat the noise as white; we multiply by beta.

WASP-18 b is the hottest planet here, so its day side emits enough to be seen as a dip when it goes behind the star. This is an external check: Shporer et al. measured 341 ppm on different data. The agreement is within 1 sigma.

Pont, Zucker and Queloz 2006 showed that correlated noise makes transit parameters less precise than white-noise errors suggest. beta is the ratio of the measured to the white-noise rms in bins of about the transit duration. Our quoted errors include detrending and MCMC but not beta.
